title: That you may believe (John 20:24–31)
hook: Thomas says my Lord and my God, and John tells us why he wrote

segments.voice: Yesterday, a locked room, and his first words. Your line was peace be with you. Did you start a hard conversation with peace? Day six hundred fifty-three.

One of the twelve wasn't in the room that Sunday. Thomas, called the twin. When the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he gives a no that people still quote. Unless I see the nail prints, and put my finger in them, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. Later readers gave him a nickname: Doubting Thomas. The Gospel never calls him that. And a week later, he's the one who says the words this Gospel opened with, to Jesus's face.
screen: `UNLESS I SEE, I WILL NOT BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Eight days later they're in the room again, doors shut, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus stands among them, says peace be with you, and turns straight to Thomas. He offers exactly what Thomas asked for: reach here your finger, behold my hands, reach your hand into my side. And then: be not faithless, but believing. Here's what's striking. The text never says Thomas touched him. Painters, like Caravaggio, show his finger in the wound. John doesn't. What John records is the answer. In the King James Bible: "And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God." Remember how this Gospel began: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. Now, near the end, the disciple who asked for proof says it to his face. The book has come full circle. Then Jesus: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." That line isn't about Thomas. It's about everyone after him, everyone reading. And then John stops and tells you why he wrote: "many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book: But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name." Not to win an argument. That you might have life. It reads like an ending, and some readers think it once was one, with chapter twenty-one added after. Tradition says Thomas later carried the news east, as far as India, where the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to him.
screen: `MY LORD AND MY GOD: FULL CIRCLE.`
`WHY JOHN WROTE: THAT YOU MIGHT HAVE LIFE.`
then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HAVE NOT SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read verse thirty-one. Settle, and breathe. Let the words come slowly: these are written, that ye might believe, and that believing ye might have life through his name. Say the last part again: that ye might have life. Notice where you're hungry for life right now: more energy, more meaning, more joy. Let the verse sit beside that hunger. If you pray, you can ask for that life. If you have doubts, Thomas's honesty is welcome here too. The bell holds the time.
That you may believe. John's own reason for writing: these signs are written so you might believe, and believing, have life.
Your line: that you might have life. Today, do one thing that makes you more alive, and if you have an honest question, say it out loud, like Thomas. Day six hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Thomas on the Sunday after Easter, and Christians in India's Saint Thomas tradition honor him as the apostle who brought them the faith.

myth: John's Gospel calls him Doubting Thomas
the nickname came later. the text calls him Thomas, called Didymus.
the text says Thomas put his finger in the wounds
Jesus invites him to, but John records only his answer: my Lord and my God.
John says he left many other signs out of his book
"many other signs truly did Jesus... which are not written in this book."

fork.setup: you're Thomas. the risen Jesus stands in front of you and offers his wounds. what do you do?
options: reach out and touch the wounds first.
say: my Lord and my God.
fork.reveal: John records only his answer: "My Lord and my God." whether he touched, the text doesn't say.

original.script: ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου
original.say: hoh KOO-ree-os moo kai hoh theh-OS moo
original.note: Greek: my Lord and my God. Thomas's confession.

trapdoor: what you thought: Thomas is the one who doubted.
what it means: the disciple who asked for proof calls Jesus my God to his face, and John tells you why he wrote it.
what a scholar hears: 'my God' circles back to 1:1, 20:30–31 reads like an original ending, and manuscripts differ in 20:31 between 'that you may come to believe' and 'that you may go on believing'.

notes: Caravaggio, The Incredulity of Saint Thomas (c. 1601–02), shows the finger in the wound. Confirm.
Textual variant at 20:31: pisteusete (aorist) vs pisteuete (present). Confirm the trapdoor wording.
Chapter 21 as a later epilogue: widely held but not universal. Stated as 'many scholars'. Confirm.
Thomas in India: tradition (Acts of Thomas; Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala). Stated as tradition.
Practice: the outline says 'read verse 31'; the practice reads it slowly. The 'my Lord and my God' original is a phrase, not one word; Keeper may prefer null.
